Professor, Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability
Associate Director, Data Institute for Societal Challenges




Ph.D., Forest Ecology, Oregon State University
M.S., Quantitative Resource Management, University of Washington
B.A., Environmental Science, University of Virginia




Dr. Mike Wimberly is a Professor in the Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability at the University of Oklahoma and the head of the EcoGRAPH research group. His research combines ecological models with satellite Earth observations to address scientific questions and develop applications in the fields of public health and natural resource management. Areas of study include wildfire and vegetation dynamics in temperate and tropical forest ecosystems, drivers and consequences of urbanization and agricultural expansion, and the effects of land use and climate on vector-borne disease transmission. Dr. Wimberly builds upon this research to create software that applies geospatial data and analytics for decision support. He has developed disease early warning systems to predict West Nile virus outbreaks in the United States and malaria in Ethiopia, used Earth observations to monitor forest degradation and urban growth in West Africa, and designed spatial simulation models to project future landscapes under scenarios of global change.

title: EPIDEMIA
text:
Outbreaks of malaria are often linked to climate variations and land use changes that affect the life cycles of the mosquito vector and the Plasmodium parasite. Early warning of the timing and locations of these epidemics can facilitate more effective targeting of resources for disease prevention, control, and treatment. We have developed the Epidemic Prognosis Incorporating Disease and Environmental Monitoring for Integrated Assessment (EPIDEMIA) system to support malaria forecasting in epidemic-prone regions of Ethiopia. EPIDEMIA uses machine-learning techniques with malaria surveillance data and environmental data from Earth-observing satellites to determine the relationships between climate variations and malaria outbreaks. The system provides an open-source software toolbox for data harmonization, predictive analytics, and report generation implemented in the R language and software environment. Remotely sensed data are accessed through a Google Earth Engine application that supports cloud-based data processing and produces downloadable summaries for use with EPIDEMIA. The software is usable with existing public health surveillance databases and can be run on a variety of computer systems.
 Examples of remotely-sensed environment data used in EPIDEMIA, including MODIS land surface temperature (left), and rainfall data from the Global Precipitation Mission (Right).
The first step in implementing EPIDEMIA is to acquire historical epidemiological and environmental data for the region of interest and develop a harmonized dataset for modeling. These data are then used to identify geographic strata for modeling and calibrate the predictive models. To generate weekly forecasts, the system is updated with recent data, model predictions are generated for the upcoming twelve weeks, and the results are used to generate a formatted report with maps and charts. Forecasting is fully automated, and the necessary data processing, modeling, and report generation steps are carried out by running a single script. A separate validation module can be used to generate retrospective forecasts and evaluate their predictive skill using historical data.
 Flowchart of the EPIDEMIA system illustrating the steps for generating a weekly forecast.
EPIDEMIA 1.0 was developed by an interdisciplinary team that includes scientists from the University of Oklahoma, along with collaborators from Ethiopian public health agencies, non-governmental organizations, and universities. The system was piloted and tested through a demonstration project in the Amhara region of Ethiopia. We worked with the United States Agency for International Development and the U.S. President’s Malaria Initiative to develop a roadmap for scaling up malaria early warning with EPIDEMIA to a national level. This work evaluated national-level malaria surveillance datasets, and engaged with a variety of stakeholders in Ethiopia. This page provides links to project outputs, including software code, documentation, and data.
We are currently working on a NASA-supported project to develop an updated version of the software that will provide substantial upgrades. The main objectives of this work are to improve the user interface to streamline modeling and provide interactive visualization for decision support, integrate new sources of environmental data from satellite Earth observations, incorporate novel predictive AI approaches for outbreak detection and forecasting, and expand the scope to include additional climate sensitive diseases besides malaria. For more information visit the EPIDEMIA 2.0 page.

title: ArboMAP
text:
West Nile virus (WNV) is endemic in the United States and poses a persistent threat to public health. In particular, the Northern Great Plains are a hot spot for WNV transmission, and South Dakota has the highest long-term incidence of West Nile neuroinvasive disease in the country. We have conducted research on WNV epidemiology to explore the environmental risk factors that affect transmission to humans. The spatial and temporal distributions of vector mosquitoes and bird hosts, and the risk of disease in humans, are strongly influenced by temperature, humidity, vegetation, soils, and land use. These relationships can be quantified using mathematical models and applied to develop maps of WNV risk and forecast the probability of future outbreaks.
 Conceptual diagram of information flow through the ArboMAP system.
We have applied these results to develop a WNV early warning system for South Dakota that combines environmental monitoring with mosquito surveillance to produce weekly maps of WNV risk during the transmission season. The Arbovirus Mapping and Prediction (ArboMAP) system ingests gridded meteorological data using Google Earth Engine, a cloud-based platform for Earth science data analysis. Mosquito abundance and testing data are uploaded from locations throughout the state via a web-based surveillance platform. Statistical models are used to estimate the mosquito infection rate from recent surveillance data, and to predict the number of human cases based on mosquito infection rate, temperature, and humidity. These models are implemented using the R programming language and software environment, and all code is publicly available via GitHub. This work is supported in part by a grant from the NASA Applied Sciences Public Health and Air Quality Program (NNX15AF74G).
 Prospective WNV forecasts. Black line/Gray shading: prediction with 95% intervals; Red line: Observed cases in 2016 or 2017; Dashed line: Observed cases in 2012; Dotted line: Observed cases in 2015.

title: CHANGE
text:
Climate change has myriad effects on ecosystems worldwide, with natural and human-caused disturbances serving as major drivers. In addition, increasing human exploitation of fire-prone ecosystems is altering fire regimes, increasing human vulnerability, and limiting management options. To better understand the implications of these changes, there is a need for simulation models that can project future landscape dynamics in the context of changing climates and expanding human populations. We developed an integrated land change simulator by coupling a model of natural disturbances and vegetation dynamics (LADS, the LAndscape Dynamics Simulator developed by Mike Wimberly) with a model of human driven land use and land cover change (FORE-SCE, the FOREcasting SCEnarios of future land cover model developed by Terry Sohl at the USGS Center for Earth Resources Observation and Science). The result is a novel model for Simulating Coupled Human and Natural Environments (CHANGE).
 Conceptual diagram of the CHANGE simulation model.
The CHANGE model simulates gridded landscapes classified into discrete land use and land cover (LULC) classes such as developed land, forest, shrubland, and cropland. Transitions between these LULC classes are modeled using a demand-allocation algorithm that was adapted from FOR-SCE. Naturally-vegetated LCLU classes are further divided into vegetation states that represent unique combinations of vegetation structure and species composition. Within these naturally-vegetated areas, succession is modeled deterministically using a state-and-transition model, and wildfires are modeled using a stochastic cellular fire spread algorithm derived from LADS. CHANGE also includes new components for explicitly modeling the human-natural interface (HNI) as a hybrid LULC class. Examples of the HNI include low-density housing in fire-prone forests in the western United States and small-scale agricultural encroachment into tropical forests in West Africa.
 Output of the CHANGE model with examples of landscape change in the Colorado Front Range: A) Wildland-urban interface expansion, B) Wildfire in the Wildland-urban interface, C) Urban growth, and D) Wildfire outside of the wildland-urban interface.
Note: CHANGE is no longer under active development. Historical code, executables, and parameter files for example scenarios are archived on GitHub.

title: Landscape Epidemiolgoy
text:
Land cover and land use influence infectious disease transmission by shaping the habitats of disease vectors and reservoir hosts and affecting human exposure to pathogens. Vegetation, hydrology, and built environments determine habitat suitability, while human activities such as urbanization, agriculture, and resource extraction modify natural habitats and create new opportunities for disease transmission. Land cover also influences local microclimates, potentially allowing vectors and hosts to persist in regions where broader climatic conditions would otherwise be unsuitable.
 Map of the relative risk of West Nile virus in South Dakota derived from a machine learning model that predicts georeferenced cases using remotely sensed environmental indices (Hess et al. 2018).
Our research has demonstrated how landscape characteristics influence the spatial distribution of mosquito-borne diseases across diverse geographic settings. In the northern Great Plains of the United States, we found that West Nile virus (WNV) incidence was highest in rural valleys dominated by grasslands and lowest in urban and forested mountainous regions (Chuang et al., 2012; Hess et al., 2018). In the Amhara region of Ethiopia, malaria incidence was highest in districts with extensive wetland cover (Midekisa et al. 2014). However, a more localized analysis of malaria transmission in four Ethiopian districts revealed different patterns, with higher incidence in areas characterized by sparse vegetation and particular patterns of human settlement (McMahon et al. 2021). Together, these studies demonstrate that landscape characteristics are important predictors of mosquito-borne disease risk, but their effects depend on geographic context and spatial scale. These findings also highlight the value of satellite Earth observations for identifying environmental risk factors and developing geographically tailored disease risk maps.

title: Urban Expansion Dynamics
text:
The world’s population is continuing to become more urbanized, particularly in low and middle-income countries located in the global South. During the 21st century, urbanization rates in Africa have increased considerably as rapidly growing populations have migrated to cities for economic opportunities. Although research has tended to focus on the largest “megacities”, there are also many rapidly growing secondary cities that are smaller in size but more numerous. The EcoGRAPH group is using satellite remote sensing to map historical patterns of urban growth in Africa and India. These data will be used to parameterize spatially explicit urban growth models for making future projections of urban expansion (Korah et al. 2024). These projections will provide a basis for assessing how expanding cities will interact with the changing climate to influence human exposure to heat and infectious diseases.
To map regional patterns of urban expansion in West Africa, we developed novel technique that more accurately capture the growth of smaller secondary cities than global land cover products (Korah and Wimberly, 2024b). Using twenty years of historical data, we showed that secondary cities were growing faster than larger primary cities, exhibiting more sprawing growth, and accounting for an increasing proportion of the total developed land cover (Korah and Wimberly, 2024a). A mixed methods study conducted in Ghana found that secondary cities had lower land and rent costs and more diverse land allocations than primary cities, creating more opportunities for developers as well as individuals seeking housing (Korah et al. 2025). Rapid urban expansion was found to be a major contributor to regional tree cover loss in both Ghana and Nigeria, accounting for 42% of this change area despite occupying only 74% of the study area (Korah and Wimberly 2026).

title: Wildfire and Tropical Forest Loss
text:
West African tropical forests are highly vulnerable to human-driven environmental change. They have the highest temperatures and longest dry seasons of all tropical forest systems worldwide. The region is under enormous pressure from a rapidly growing human population and its demands for agricultural production, as well as wood and other forest products. Much of the original native forest cover has been lost, and the remnants are at risk from logging, agricultural encroachment, and wildfires. Our work has documented the increasing susceptibility of West African forests to degradation, developed techniques for monitoring these changes with remote sensing, built models to predict the risk of future degradation and deforestation, and quantitied the long-term impacts of degradation on forest carbon storage.
In West Africa, spatial patterns of active fire detections and burned area are mainly influenced by vegetation, whereas the seasonality and intensity of fires are more strongly associated with climate (Dwomoh and Wimberly 2017). Between 2003-2015, fire activity generally decreased in the savanna ecoregions but increased in the forested ecoregions. A broader analyis of forests throughout the moist African tropics also found increasing trends of active fire detections that were associated with increasing temperature, vapor pressure deficit, and deforestation (Wimberly et al. 2024). In the tropical forest reserves of Ghana, we found that forest degradation caused by fire and other disturbances increases the risk of subsequent fire, raising concerns that increasing droughts resulting from climate change will catalyze new cycles of wildfire and forest loss (Dwomoh et al. 2019). In these forests, degradation occurs through a positive feedback loop of declining canopy cover and increasing fire frequency, eventually leading to the establishment of fire-prone vegetation dominated by grasses and invasive shrubs (Dwomoh and Wimberly 2017).
Across the Upper Guinean Region of West Africa, we have documented broad trends of decreasing woody vegetation and increasing herbaceous vegetation cover (Liu et al. 2017). Using a time series analysis of Landsat imagery, we developed a historical database of disturbances across all forest reserves of Ghana from 2003 to 2019 (Wimberly et al. 2022). Rates of forest degradation, loss, and recovery were relatively low from 2003 to 2015, followed by a sharp increase associated with drought and fires in 2016. Patterns of forest disturbance are highly sensitive to landscape fragmentation, human population pressure, and drought, and these variables can be used to map the relative risk of future disturbances (Wanyama et al. 2023). Biomass recovery following forest degradation is relatively slow because changes in forest structure increase the potential for subsequent fires and other disturbances (Wanyama et al. 2025).

title: Climate Epidemiology
text:
Climate is an important driver of infectious disease transmission, influencing the geographic distributions of pathogens and their hosts, the seasonal timing of transmission, and the occurrence of disease outbreaks. Understanding this variability is essential for anticipating how infectious diseases respond to short-term weather events, seasonal climate fluctuations, and long-term climate change. Our research has advanced understanding of the climatic drivers of West Nile virus (WNV) in the United States and malaria in Ethiopia and India. Studies of WNV outbreaks in the northern Great Plains demonstrated that disease incidence was highest in areas with warmer temperatures and intermediate precipitation (Wimberly et al. 2008), while subsequent research identified elevated temperatures during both winter and the transmission season as important predictors of outbreaks (Wimberly et al. 2014). Time-series modeling in South Dakota and Louisiana further demonstrated the importance of temperature, precipitation, atmospheric humidity, and wind speed in explaining seasonal and interannual variation in WNV transmission (Davis et al. 2018, Bump et al. 2025).
 Data from the Ahmara Region of Ethiopia illustrating seasonal patterns of temperature and precipitation and their associations with malaria cases (Midekisa et al. 2015).
An important contribution of this work has been demonstrating that the climatic drivers of disease transmission vary across geographic and environmental settings. For example, our research in Ethiopia showed that temperature was a stronger predictor of malaria outbreaks in wetter districts, whereas rainfall and moisture conditions were more influential in drier districts (Midekisa et al. 2015). In the United States, temperature and humidity had positive effects on WNV occurence in a cooler and drier climate versus negative effects in a warmer and more humid climate Bump et al. 2025). These findings highlight the importance of accounting for local environmental conditions rather than assuming that climate–disease relationships are uniform across regions. This research has established a foundation for climate-informed disease forecasting and early warning systems. By integrating environmental observations with disease surveillance data, we have developed predictive models that account for delayed responses to weather conditions and spatial variation in climatic drivers (Midekisa et al. 2012; Davis et al. 2019). These approaches provide a scientific basis for anticipating disease outbreaks and supporting more proactive public health surveillance and response. For more information see the sections on Malaria Early Warning and West Nile Virus Forecasting.

title: Malaria Early Warning
text:
Malaria remains one of the most significant public health challenges in many low- and middle-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. To make surveillance a more effective and efficient core intervention, there is a need to shift from reactive to predictive approaches by using models to forecast malaria risk. Our work on malaria early warning systems has involved developing and testing predictive models for malaria forecasting and outbreak detection in the epidemic-prone Amhara region of Ethiopia (Midekisa et al. 2012, Davis et al. 2019, Nekorchuk et al. 2021). These studies have emphasized the importance of accounting for spatial heterogeneity in the lagged effects of climate drivers. We have also evaluated the accuracy of different sources of geospatial environmental data (Alemu and Wimberly 2020) and developed informatics tools to facilitate access to satellite Earth observations for malaria early warning (Liu et al. 2015, Wimberly et al. 2022).
Working with partners in the Ethiopian public health sector, we co-developed the Epidemic Prognosis Incorporating Disease and Environmental Modeling for Integrated Assessment (EPIDEMIA) system for implementing malaria forecasting (Merkord et al. 2017). We conducted a pilot study implementing EPIDEMIA in the Ahmara region and conducted a scoping study to develop a roadmap for scaling malaria early warning to a national level (Wimberly and Nekorchuk 2021). EPIDEMIA is programmed using the R language adn environment for statistical computing, and the code is freely available on GitHub. Visit the EPIDEMIA page for more links to the software and documentation. We are currently developing EPIDEMIA 2.0, a next-generation version of EPIDEMIA with an improved user interface and enhanced capabilities for malaria modeling and prediction.

title: Mosquito Ecology
text:
Mosquito abundance, behavior, and transmission potential are sensitive to multiple environmental factors. Larvae require suitable aquatic habitats, and adults use a variety of natural and human-created structures for resting habitats. Because mosquitoes are small ectotherms, their body temperature and associated vital rates are dependent on ambient temperature. Further, their moisture relations are strongly influenced by thermal conditions and atmospheric humidity (Brown et al. 2023, Huxley et al. 2026). These environmental relationships vary depending on the mosquito species and the environmental context.
In South Dakota, Aedes vexans, a floodwater mosquito, is associated with webland habitats and increases in abundance when heavy rainfall results in widespread surface water (Chuang et al. 2011; Chuang et al. 2012). In contrast, Culex tarsalis, an important vector of West Nile virus, is associated with grassland habitats and has a weak relationship with rainfall and a much stronger. relationship with temperature. In Oklahoma, Culex quinquefasciatus is most abundant in landscapes with high densities of buildings and roads, whereas Aedes albopictus is most abundant in landscapes with low tree cover (McMahon et al. 2022).
the abundances of Culex quinquefasciatus and Aedes albopictus are highest on warm, humid days with little precipitation in the previous two weeks . In Georgia, variation in land cover creates distinctive microclimates that influence the mosquito reproduction, growth, and survival as well as transmission and development rates of mosquito-borne pathogens, creating localized “hot spots” of high disease transmission potential (Wimberly et al. 2020).
Although most research on weather and mosquitoes uses standard meteorological variables such as temperature, humidity, and precipitation, other variables such as drought indices, soil moisture, and solar radiation may have stronger associations with mosquito abundance (Bump and Wimberly, 2026). Similarly, remotely sensed environmental measurements from Earth observing satellites, such as surface water cover, vegetation indices, and land surface temeprature, have been shown to perform as well as or better than ground-based meteorological measurements as predictors of mosquito abundance (Chuang et al. 2012; McMahon et al. 2022).Our research emphasizes the importance of determining the specific hydrometeorological factors that influence mosquito biology and measuring them at scales that are relevant for mosquito ecology.

title: Urban Health
text:
Urban environments are the fastest growing landscapes on the planet, and transmission of diseases by urban adapted mosquitoes has increased markedly over the past several decades. The EcoGRAPH group is involved in several projects focused on mapping mosquito habitats and microclimates in cities, modeling the distribution of urban disease transmission hotspots, and projecting the future changes in transmission risk resulting from urban growth and climate change. We used satellite remote sensing and in situ microclimate measurements to generate high-resolution maps of temperature and linked them with mechanistic transmission models to estimate the localized patterns of potential dengue transmission in the southeastern U.S. (Wimberly et al. 2020).
We are currently collaborating with Courtney Murdock (Cornell University) and Mercedes Pascual (University of Chicago) to extend these approaches to map neighborhood-level patterns of urban malaria transmission by Anopheles stephensi in Indian cities of Ahmedabad and Gujarat. This work will extend existing temperature-trait modeling approaches to incorporate the influences of humidity on water balance in mosquitoes. We established a network of indoor and outdoor microclimate sensors located at residential homes and have characterized spatial and temporal microclimate patterns and their land cover associations (Jamal et al. 2025). We conducted a survey to assess the the interrelationships between socioeconomic factors, domestic water management practices, and malaria (Batheja et al. 2026). These data are currently being used to develop multifactor spatial models to predict malaria risk across both cities. We also collaborated with partners in Ethiopia to study malaria trends in urbanized settings and evaluate implications of Anopheles stephensi invasion for urban malaria control (Teka et al. 2023).

title: Pyrogeography of the Western United States
text:
Wildfires in western North America have increased in size and intensity over the past several decades because of climate change and landscape alterations that have affected ignitions and fuels. The EcoGRAPH group has studied the effects of climate, vegetation, and forest management on wildfire in the western United States (Liu and Wimberly 2015) and developed models to project the effects of climate change on future fire regimes (Liu and Wimberly 2016). These studies projected increased burned area and showed that the indirect effects of shifting vegetation types in response to climate change will be as important as the direct effects of climate change on fire weather and fuel moisture. We also projected the impacts of climate change and wildland-urban interface (WUI) expansion on fire risk in the Colorado Front Range (Liu et al. 2015). The combined effects of these two factors were non-linear, with climate change exacerbating the risks from the expansion of low-density homes into fire-prone vegetation types.
Fuel treatments, such as thinning and prescribed burning, are a potentially valuable tool for adapting to changing fire regimes. We used satellite remote sensing data and fire behavior models to analyze the effects of different types of fuel treatments on wildfire size and severity (Wimberly et al. 2009, Cochrane et al. 2012). Treatments that combined the reduction of canopy fuels by thinning with the reduction of surface fuels by prescribed burning or mastication were most effective at reducing fire severities and sizes. We also explored the complex influences of forest roads on fire regimes in dry forests of eastern Washington, USA. Both human and lightning ignitions were more frequent close to roads than in more remote areas (Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2012). However, fires frequently stopped spreading near roads (Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2011), and fire severity also tended to be lower in the vicinity of roads (Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2013).
In the Pacific Northwest region of the United States, old-growth forests are characterized by large tree sizes, accumulations of dead wood, and complex horizontal and vertical structure. The extent of old-growth forests was greatly reduced by logging during the 20th century (Wimberly and Ohmann 2004). However, large wildfires occurred in the region prior to European settlement, raising the question of how current levels of old growth compare to those under pre-settlement fire regimes. To answer this question, we developed the Landscape Dynamics Simulator (LADS) to simulate wildfires and the dynamics of old-growth forests in historical landscapes (Wimberly et al. 2000, Wimberly 2002). Despite the occurrence of large wildfires, we found that old growth was historically the most prevalent age class, covering 29-52% of the total forest area. The current area of old-growth forest is considerably lower than this historical range of variability (Wimberly et al. 2004). More recent versions of LADS have been modified to better model the dynamics of mixed-severity fire regimes (Wimberly and Kennedy 2008, Kennedy and Wimberly 2009). In the future, a warmer and drier climate will result in increased fire frequencies and severities that will push landscapes even further outside the range of historical variability (Wimberly and Liu 2014).

title: West Nile Virus Forecasting
text:
West Nile virus is the most common mosquito-borne disease in the United States, causing more than 53,000 reported disease cases and 2,500 deaths since it was introduced in 1999. The Northern Great Plains have consistently been a hot spot of WNV incidence, with most cases concentrated in a few specific locations and occurring in a small number of outbreak years (Wimberly et al. 2013). Because of the relatively short disease transmission season, weather conditions in the spring and early summer influence the rate of virus amplification in mosquitoes and avian hosts and the subsequent risk of spillover into human populations (Wimberly et al. 2014). We developed a regional forecasting model that predicted WNV cases as a function of the rates of vegetation greenup and degree day accumulation during spring and summer (Chuang and Wimberly, 2012). This model was later refined to increase accuracy by incorporating both meteorological variables and mosquito infection rates as predictors (Davis et al. 2017, 2018).
The approach was implemented as the Arbovirus Monitoring and Prediction (ArboMAP) system, which has been used to forecast WNV in South Dakota beginning in 2016 (Nekorchuk et al. 2023). A retrospective validation of ArboMAP forecasts in South Dakota found that integrating environmental data with mosquito surveillance data increased prediction accuracy and that accurate forecasts would be made early enough in the season to inform disease prevention and mosquito control activities prior to the peak of human transmission (Wimberly et al. 2022). Visit the ArboMAP page for links to the software and documentation. Our team is building the next generation ArboMAP 2.0, which introduces an enhanced user experience, new data streams, and more powerful modeling and prediction tools.

title: Grassland Conservation
text:
The prairies of North America are among the most threatened terrestrial ecosystems on the continent. Increasing corn and soybean production has led to substantial conversion of grasslands to row crop agriculture at the western edge of the U.S. Corn Belt in North Dakota and South Dakota. Much of this change is occurring in the Prairie Pothole Region, which has a high density of shallow wetlands and provides critical habitat for numerous migratory bird species. Grasslands provide multiple ecosystem services, including the maintenance of pollinator communities, long-term carbon sequestration, prevention of soil and nutrient loss, and protection of water quality. Loss and fragmentation of grassland cover reduce the amount and quality of habitat for a variety of insects, amphibians, and birds. The EcoGRAPH group uses satellite remote sensing and geospatial analysis to quantify patterns of grassland loss throughout the region as well as the drivers and ecological impacts of these changes.
We documented more than 500,000 ha of grassland loss in the western Corn Belt between 2007 and 2011 (Wright and Wimberly, 2013). Although most of the converted grasslands were former croplands enrolled in the conservation reserve program, nearly 20% were undisturbed native grasslands (Wimberly et al. 2017). Larger farms, younger farm operators, higher levels of farm income, higher proportions of rented croplands, and marginal yields were associated with higher rates of cropland expansion and grassland conversion. In eastern South Dakota, the remaining native grasslands are highly fragmented, with major habitat concentrations connected by narrow corridors of “stepping stone” patches (Wimberly et al. 2018).
Another widspread threat to grasslands in the Great Plains is encroachment by woody plants, including eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana). We have implemented novel methods for rapid assessment of eastern red cedar cover using satellite remote sensing (Kaskie et al. 2019) and developed a modeling approach for mapping low density stands where red cedar is currently invading (Kaskie et al. 2022). These techniques can help to quantify the extent of grasslands impacted by red cedar enroachment and target areas of recent spread for proactive management.

title: Rural Health
text:
We mapped obesity and associated risk factors at a county level for the conterminous United States, and we analyzed their relationships with supermarket accessibility (Michimi and Wimberly 2010b). The prevalence of obesity increased with distance to supermarkets in metropolitan counties, but no relationship was found in non-metropolitan counties (Michimi and Wimberly 2010a). An analysis of obesity rates in major U.S. cities similarly found positive associations with the proportions of supermarket and full-service restaurants and negatively associated with fast-food and convenience stores (Michimi and Wimberly 2015). In non-metropolitan counties, physical activity was highest and obesity was lowest in counties with abundant recreational opportunities, including parks, trails, and other outdoor amenities (Michimi and Wimberly 2012). This work shows that obesity is sensitive to the local food environment, but also highlights different effects in urban versus rural settings and provides evidence for broader effects of the physical environmental and associated recreational amenities.
Rural isolation and accessibility of health care can also have substantial impacts on health outcomes following a cancer diagnosis. In South Dakota, one of the most sparsely populated U.S. states, isolated rural communities, which also had high levels of economic deprivation, had an increased risk of late-stage colorectal cancer diagnosis (Lin and Wimberly 2017). Patients with better geographic access to radiation therapy facilities were found to have a higher probability of receiving radiation therapy versus mastectomy as treatment for breast cancer (Lin and Wimberly 2018). These results highlight the challenges of accessing health care in isolated rural environments and their effects on cancer outcomes.

title: Tick-Borne Pathogens
text:
Ticks are blood-sucking arthropods that transmit a variety of disease-causing pathogens. These pathogens are typically sustained in enzootic cycles involving multiple host species and transmitted to humans through infected tick bites. Ehrlichia chaffeensis and Anaplasma phagocytophilum are common tick-borne pathogens in the southern United States, each associated with a different tick vector and distinctive set of host species. Their geographic ranges are associated with multiple climate and land cover variables (Yabsley et al. 2005). However, the most important environmental predictors vary geographically, reflecting distinctive ecological conditions in different parts of the species’ ranges (Wimberly et al. 2008b). Climate is the main determinant of pathogen presence in the eastern U.S., whereas forest cover and fragmentation constrain the western range boundaries. In the Mississippi Alluvial Valley, there are strong effects of forest cover and flooding (Manangan et al. 2007). Bayesian hierarchical models that include environmental predictors with spatially varying coefficients and conditional autoregressive terms can accurately predict the regional distributions of both pathgens (Wimberly et al. 2008a). This work showed that it is possible to model the geographic distributions of tick-borne pathogens in sentinel hosts and emphasize the importance of accounting for spatially heterogeneity and spatial autocorrelation to account for their complex environmental relationships.

title: EcoGRAPH
text: The EcoGRAPH team is in the Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability at the University of Oklahoma. Our research explores the impacts of changing climate and landscapes on ecosystems and human health, with an emphasis on developing spatial decision support tools to support public health decisions, land use planning, and natural resource management. We address these topics through landscape, regional, and global analyses using satellite remote sensing and other sources of environmental monitoring data. Specific research areas include the effects of environmental change on vector-borne disease outbreaks, the influences of human land use and wildfires on forest landscape dynamics, the impacts of agricultural expansion and intensification on native ecosystems, and the development of computer software for disease outbreak forecasting and landscape change modeling. We conduct our research in locations throughout the world, including North America, West Africa, Ethiopia, and India.

title: ArboMAP 2.0
text:
Arthropod-borne viruses such as West Nile virus (WNV) impose significant public health burdens across the United States. Although environmental drivers of transmission are well understood and forecasting techniques have advanced rapidly, operational uptake remains limited by fragmented tools, inconsistent workflows, and barriers to scalability. Building on more than a decade of development and real-world implementation, this project will create ArboMAP 2.0, a next-generation, nationally scalable platform for arbovirus risk forecasting and decision support. The goal is to transform ArboMAP from a successful regional forecasting system into a widely accessible, interoperable platform serving stakeholders at CDC and state and local health departments nationwide.
ArboMAP 2.0 will provide a unified, infrastructure for generating actionable forecasts of arbovirus risk across diverse ecological and institutional settings. The effort will combine technical modernization with coordinated stakeholder engagement to ensure the platform is scientifically robust, operationally relevant, and widely adopted. We will redesign the application with a modern, user-centered interface with simplified workflows, automated data ingestion, and clear visualization of risk and uncertainty to reduce barriers to adoption and support real-time decision-making. Modern software design frameworks will make it straightforward to deploy in the cloud, on local networks, or on individual workstations. Improved data integration with NASA Earth science datasets and public health surveillance will enable interoperability with a variety of public health data systems. The updated framework will support modular workflows that allow adaptation to multiple pathogens, locations, and data environments. Flexible model pipelines will accommodate new data types and emerging machine learning and AI modeling techniques.
A central component of this effort will be building a national community of ArboMAP users and contributors. We will develop connections with national and state health departments to co-develop use cases and pilot deployments. A user network will be established to share best practices in arbovirus forecasting and public health response. Training, documentation, and implementation toolkits will be tailored to the needs of public health practitioners. By lowering technical barriers and fostering a community of practice, the project will accelerate the translation of forecasting science into routine public health action. The resulting infrastructure will support earlier detection of outbreaks and better targeting vector control and disease prevention efforts. More broadly, this effort will provide a model for transforming forecasting models informed by NASA data into durable, national public health capabilities.

title: EPIDEMIA 2.0
text:
In Ethiopia, confirmed malaria cases have increased threefold since 2019. This resurgence is driven by multiple factors, including conflict, drug and insecticide resistance, and climate fluctuations. There is currently a strong demand for integrated surveillance and forecasting tools that can predict future outbreaks and allow proactive interventions to reduce outbreak severity. To address this needs, the Epidemic Prognosis Incorporating Disease and Environmental Monitoring for Integrated Assessment (EPIDEMIA) system was co-developed by a team us U.S. and Ethiopian scientists and public health professionals. EPIDEMIA is a suite of software tools uses forecasting models driven by NASA Earth Observations to predict epidemics associated with climate fluctuations. Advanced outbreak detection algorithms are also applied to predict epidemics driven by non-climatic factors. The system has been tested and piloted at a regional level, and the opportunities and barriers associated with broader implementation have been assessed. To support scale up, there is a need to enhance EPIDEMIA by expanding the utilization of NASA Earth observations, increasing forecasting accuracy, and improving the end user experience. The overarching goal of this project is to develop EPIDEMIA 2.0, a next-generation software system, by achieving the following objectives.

Improve the user interface to streamline the modeling process and support interactive visualization for decision support,
Integrate new sources of environmental data from satellite Earth observations,
Incorporate multiple modeling approaches for outbreak detection and forecasting, and
Include additional climate-sensitive diseases besides malaria.

This work builds upon previous work that included basic research to understand climate-malaria relationships, the development of software tools for predicting malaria, and engaging with public health stakeholders to understand the opportunities and barriers associated with national-level implementation of these tools. The research proposed here will substantially extend the previous work by supporting the sustainable expansion of EPIDEMIA throughout Ethiopia, incorporating additional streams of Earth observation data to enhance predictions, and extending the approach to other climate-sensitive diseases.

title: WAForDD
text:
The West Africa Forest Degradation Data system (WAForDD) was developed to provide annual estimates of canopy cover change in the forest reserves of Ghana. The system uses a historical Landsat imagery to generate a time series of canopy cover from 2001-present, along with disturbance and recovery rates from 2003-present. Canopy cover is estimated using a random forests machine learning algorithm and extensive training and validation datasets derived from very-high resolution satellite imagery. The LandTrendr temporal segmentation is then applied to the canopy cover time series for each pixel to distinguish forest disturbance and recovery from periods of relative stability. We found that this approach can detect forest degradation that results in partial canopy removal as well as complete forest loss and post-disturbance recovery. Canopy cover remained relatively stable in protected areas such as National Parks, but was reduced by forest degradation and loss from logging, fire, illegal mining, and agricultural encroachment in many of the other forest reserves.
 Closed canopy forest in the Bobiri Reserve, Ghana.
WAForDD is implemented using Google Earth Engine (GEE), a cloud-based platform for geospatial analysis that provides access to the Landsat archive as well as many other Earth observation datasets. GEE has enabled the transfer of WAForDD to partners organization in Ghana by providing access to data and code through a cloud-based integrated development environment. This approach eliminates the need to download, store, and process large volumes of remote sensing imagery on local systems. We also developed a stand-alone Earth Engine App to facilitate data visualization and summarization. GEE programmers can explore the code archive and read the project documentation for more detailed information. Those wishing to explore the annual change data in more detail should use the WaforDD App.
We have collaborated with our partners to continue updating WAForDD anually. The remote sensing methods and validation of the forest degradation dataset are documented in a peer-reviewed journal article (Wimberly et al. 2022). The WAForDD dataset has been applied in several research projects, including a study of the drivers of fire and non-fire disturbances (Wanyama et al. 2023), and an analysis of post-disturbance forest recovery rates that combined WAForDD data with forest biomass and structure data from the GEDI mission (Wanyama et al. 2025).
